# Mahānāradakassapajātaka (Ja 545)
**ID:** Ja 545
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahānāradakassapajātaka* is one of the major narratives of the *Mahānipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection (PTS Jā VI 219–255), often titled simply *Nārada-jātaka* in Southeast Asian manuscript traditions [Appleton 2010; Marino 2017]. According to its nidāna framing, the Buddha delivered the story at the Laṭṭhivana pleasure garden in connection with the conversion of Uruveḷa-Kassapa, illustrating how he had previously converted him in an earlier existence [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010]. In the narrative of the past, King Aṅgati of Videha is led astray by heretical teachers into denying the efficacy of kamma and moral consequence [Murphy; Fenn 1994; Hazra 1994]. Although his virtuous daughter attempts to dissuade him, the Bodhisatta—born as the Great Brahmā Nārada—descends from the heavens carrying a carrying-pole or yoke over his shoulders to refute the king's nihilistic doctrine, vividly depict the terrors of hell, and re-establish him in moral conduct, thereby exemplifying the Bodhisatta's perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā*) [Murphy; Appleton 2010; Hazra 1994]. The text includes extended, vivid descriptions of hell realms, complete with punishments such as the sword-leaf forest (*asipattavana*), ravenous beasts, the river Vetaraṇī, and a realm of perpetual darkness [Fenn 1994; Marino 2017].
Beyond canonical transmission, the *Mahānāradakassapajātaka* has exercised notable historical and artistic influence. Chronicles record that the elder Mahādhammarakkhita preached this jātaka to convert the region of Mahāraṭṭha following the Third Buddhist Council [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Bapat & Hirakawa 1970]. Episodes from the tale, particularly Nārada descending from the heavens with his yoke and instructing King Aṅgati, were frequently sculpted on Dvāravatī-period *sīmā* boundary stones in the Chi River valley of Northeast Thailand [Murphy]. The work also served as an important thematic model for later regional Buddhist texts, including the northern Thai *Māleyyatherasutta* [Cousins et al. 1974].
SuttaCentral notes passage-level parallels between the jātaka and the *Sukhapatthanā Sutta* (Iti 76), the *Sattigumbajātaka* (Ja 503), and a Chinese parallel in T 765.124, while noting cross-references in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (Cp 4) and *Petavatthu* (Pv 38) [SuttaCentral]. Machine alignments computed by DharmaNexus confirm extensive Pali-internal reuse, including matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, Iti 76 (§102.4–107.6), Ja 503 (§101.4–107.6), Pv 38 (§36.3–38.2), the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Pāyāsi Sutta* (DN 23, §92.1–92.3) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects cross-linguistic textual alignments with Sanskrit works (including the Patna Dharmapada, Nāgārjuna's *Suhṛllekha*, and the *Lalitavistara*), Tibetan translations (such as the *Jātakamālā* D4150 and *Karmaśataka* D0340), and Chinese Āgama discourses (T 99 and T 26) [DharmaNexus].
